content.title: Identifying Controlled Variables and Experimental Constants
content.overview: In ACT Science, success depends on distinguishing between what changes and what stays the same in an experiment. Controlled variables (or constants) are factors intentionally kept identical across all experimental groups to ensure that the results are caused only by the independent variable.
learning_objectives: Define controlled variables and experimental constants.
Distinguish controlled variables from independent and dependent variables.
Identify factors that must be held constant to prevent experimental bias or confounding results.
Verify if a specific factor qualifies as a controlled variable based on a provided experimental description.

sections.title: The Role of Constants in Scientific Investigation
sections.content: A controlled variable, also known as a constant, is any factor that is kept the same for all groups in an experiment. The purpose of controlling variables is to isolate the effect of the Independent Variable (IV) on the Dependent Variable (DV). If a factor other than the IV changes between groups, it becomes a 'confound,' making it impossible to tell if the DV changed because of the IV or because of that other factor. In ACT Science passages, look for words like 'identical,' 'same,' 'constant,' or 'uniform' to identify these elements.

sections.title: The Constant-Check Strategy
sections.content:
To accurately identify controlled variables, follow these steps: 1. Explicitly list the Independent Variable (what is being changed by the researcher). 2. Explicitly list the Dependent Variable (what is being measured). 3. Scan the experimental setup for every other factor mentioned. 4. If a factor is described as being the same for every trial or group, it is a controlled variable. If a factor varies but is not the IV, it is an uncontrolled variable that might invalidate the results.

![A flowchart showing the steps to identify controlled variables: Identify IV, Identify DV, Scan for 'Same' factors, Label as Controlled.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/1c246906-8695-4c7c-b23c-b92b175fe618-1786506633255-215.webp)

worked_examples.question: A scientist investigates how different concentrations of salt affect the boiling point of water. She uses three beakers, each containing 500 mL of distilled water. She adds 10g of salt to Beaker A, 20g to Beaker B, and 30g to Beaker C. All beakers are heated on the same model of hot plate at the same power setting. What is a controlled variable in this experiment?
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the Independent Variable (IV). Here, it is the concentration of salt (10g, 20g, 30g). Step 2: Identify the Dependent Variable (DV). This is the boiling point of the water. Step 3: Identify factors kept the same. The volume of water (500 mL), the type of water (distilled), the model of hot plate, and the power setting are all kept identical. Step 4: Select a constant. Therefore, the volume of water (500 mL) is a controlled variable.

common_mistakes: Confusing the Dependent Variable with a constant: Remember that the DV is the result you measure, which should change, while a constant must stay the same.
Assuming a variable is controlled when it isn't mentioned: Only label factors as controlled if the text explicitly states they were kept the same.
Confusing the Control Group with Controlled Variables: The control group is a baseline group; controlled variables are the specific factors (like temperature or volume) applied to all groups.
exam_tips: Look for the word 'identical' in the description of experimental apparatus or subjects.
If a question asks 'Why did the scientist use the same amount of X in all trials?', the answer is usually 'to ensure that X did not affect the results' or 'to control for X.'
In data tables, if a column has the same value for every single row, that column represents a controlled variable.
content.recap: Controlled variables are the 'anchors' of an experiment. By keeping everything except the independent variable constant, scientists ensure that their measurements of the dependent variable are valid and unbiased.

knowledge_claims.content: A controlled variable is a factor that is kept identical across all experimental groups to ensure it does not influence the dependent variable.
Unlike the independent variable, which is intentionally changed, a controlled variable must remain the same in every trial.
In an ACT Science passage, words such as 'identical,' 'same,' or 'uniform' typically signal a controlled variable.
To identify constants, first isolate the independent and dependent variables, then look for any other factors described as unchanging across groups.
If a data table shows a column where every entry is the same value, that column represents a controlled variable.
The purpose of holding variables constant is to isolate the relationship between the independent variable and the dependent variable.
It is a mistake to assume a factor is controlled if the passage does not explicitly state it was kept the same for all groups.
An experimental constant is another term for a controlled variable.
A factor is only a controlled variable if it appears identical across every experimental group or condition.
If a scientist uses the same room temperature for three different groups testing fertilizer, room temperature is a controlled variable.
A factor that varies between groups but is not the independent variable is considered an uncontrolled confound, not a controlled variable.
The dependent variable is the measured outcome and should not be confused with the controlled variables that are kept constant.

items.stem:
SCIENCE MATERIAL SET 1
Students tested how water temperature affected the time required for a tablet to dissolve. They used identical tablets, 100 mL of water in each cup, and stirred each cup at the same rate.

TABLE 1
Temperature (°C) | Dissolving time (s)
10 | 29
20 | 21
30 | 16
40 | 12

Trial 2 repeated the procedure with twice the water volume. Researcher 1 claims that higher temperature increases particle motion and therefore decreases dissolving time. Researcher 2 agrees that temperature matters but claims that stirring rate is the dominant factor whenever stirring is not controlled.

Which factor was held constant?
items.explanation: The keyed response follows the material and directly targets 识别控制变量和实验常量.
